chapter: Learning piano, dancing and Alphonso Trent
title: Benno Kennedy and Price's claim that jazz is a black tradition
summary: After praising trumpeter Benno Kennedy he rebuts the teacher who said he lacked musicality and argues jazz is rooted in black heritage.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Benno Kennedy was a trumpet player?

Oh, was he a trumpet player! He was fantastic. Benno was really nice. He played with Trent. I think he came from Wichita Falls. That's the same place that Herschel Evans came from. And...I think that playing music, Dan, can become contagious and then, if you have any insight or any...this damn guy that said that I didn't know anything about music, he's crazy. Because he didn't realize that I have this innate feeling for this stuff, you know. And that moment that the woman asked me to do--you know what I mean--to do that work, then I think that's when it was born; I just decided to let it break out--you know what I mean--and this is it, you know what I mean. What do you mean telling me that I can't...that I don't have no...I think that anybody can learn some things. For example, they say the white musicians can't play, but I don't want anybody telling me Gene Krupa wasn't a good musician. I don't want

them telling me that Benny Goodman, no matter if he was classically trained...he was a good musician. But I think because we think in the tradition of heritage, of that black heritage, that may be the thing that people have not been able to unscramble. And the writers need to determine what we're talking about. See we're talking about here...when we speak of jazz, then we speak of a thing that's a black thing. Now, that don't mean that it has to necessarily remain that. But then we think that there should be those original roots.
